title: The Order of Warmth and Competence
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece draws on social psychology research on how people judge others along two axes, warmth and competence, and argues these two dimensions are frequently sequenced differently for leaders than for everyday social relationships. In ordinary social settings, people tend to establish likeability before demonstrating expertise. For leaders specifically, the piece argues the sequence flips, audiences tolerate a leader who is less warm more readily than one who seems less competent. The takeaway is a specific sequencing recommendation, demonstrate competence first, then let warmth build on that foundation.
points: People generally judge others along two axes, warmth and competence, which research shows are often incorrectly perceived as being in tension.
In ordinary social relationships, likeability typically gets established before expertise.
For leaders specifically, the sequence flips, audiences tolerate a less-warm leader more readily than a less-competent one.
Leaders who prioritize being liked before demonstrating competence are described as more likely to be perceived as weaker.
quotes: We find more similarity, affinity, and positivity with those we experience as warm and caring. On the other hand, those we perceive as highly competent will increase our confidence and our energy to get things done.
Fascinatingly, research shows there is a tendency for people to view warmth and competence as at odds with each other.
But we hold leaders to a different standard. Leaders who work hard to be liked and to be seen as warm, relationally caring people are often seen as less competent.
If we have to accept a weaker dimension, we prefer leaders who are less likeable, as long as they are highly competent.
By demonstrating their competence first, they show people they are worth following. They give people the confidence they need to excel.
